thread|thread of execution: "a flow of execution through the process code, with its own program counter, system registers and stack"; the process concept other than resource grouping, "a thread of execution, usually shortened to just thread". See [A thread is a flow of execution with its own PC, registers and stack](#/comp4736-p4/what-is-a-thread).
lightweight process: Another name for a thread; "Threads provide a way to improve application performance through parallelism". See [A thread is a flow of execution with its own PC, registers and stack](#/comp4736-p4/what-is-a-thread).
quasi-parallel: Motivation 1, decomposing an application where "multiple activities are going on at once" into "multiple sequential threads that run in quasi-parallel" makes "the programming model … simpler". See [A thread is a flow of execution with its own PC, registers and stack](#/comp4736-p4/what-is-a-thread).
lighter weight (motivation 2): Threads "are easier and faster to create and destroy than processes. Creating a thread goes 10–100 times faster than creating a process". See [A thread is a flow of execution with its own PC, registers and stack](#/comp4736-p4/what-is-a-thread).
overlap of computing and I/O (motivation: Threads "yield no performance gain when all of them are CPU bound, but when there is substantial computing and also substantial I/O, having threads allows these activities to overlap". See [A thread is a flow of execution with its own PC, registers and stack](#/comp4736-p4/what-is-a-thread).
multiple CPUs (motivation 4): "Threads are useful on systems with multiple CPUs, where real parallelism is possible". See [A thread is a flow of execution with its own PC, registers and stack](#/comp4736-p4/what-is-a-thread).
word processor with three threads: One thread interacts with the user, one handles reformatting in the background, a third handles disk backups, e.g. automatically saving the file every few minutes. See [The word processor, the web server and three ways to build a server](#/comp4736-p4/thread-usage).
dispatcher thread: "reads incoming requests for work from the network", chooses an idle (blocked) worker thread, hands it the request and wakes it, "moving it from blocked state to ready state". See [The word processor, the web server and three ways to build a server](#/comp4736-p4/thread-usage).
worker thread: Checks whether the request "can be satisfied from the Web page cache"; if not, reads the page from disk and blocks until the disk operation completes. See [The word processor, the web server and three ways to build a server](#/comp4736-p4/thread-usage).
Web page cache: The cache in the multithreaded Web server "to which all threads have access". See [The word processor, the web server and three ways to build a server](#/comp4736-p4/thread-usage).
multithreaded Web server: A Web server process with one dispatcher thread, several worker threads and a shared Web page cache. See [The word processor, the web server and three ways to build a server](#/comp4736-p4/thread-usage).
threads server model: "Parallelism, blocking system calls". See [The word processor, the web server and three ways to build a server](#/comp4736-p4/thread-usage).
single-threaded process server|single-th: "No parallelism, blocking system calls". See [The word processor, the web server and three ways to build a server](#/comp4736-p4/thread-usage).
finite-state machine server|finite-state: "Parallelism, nonblocking system calls, interrupts". See [The word processor, the web server and three ways to build a server](#/comp4736-p4/thread-usage).
resource grouping: One of the "two independent concepts" of the process model; a process "has an address space containing program text and data, as well as other resources … open files, child processes, pending alarms, signal handlers, accounting information"; grouped "they can be managed more easily". See [Resource grouping versus execution: what is shared and what is private](#/comp4736-p4/classical-thread-model).
execution: The other concept of the process model, the thread. See [Resource grouping versus execution: what is shared and what is private](#/comp4736-p4/classical-thread-model).
no protection between threads: Every thread can access every address in the process, so "one thread can read, write, or even wipe out another thread's stack"; no protection "because (1) it is impossible, and (2) it should not be necessary". See [Resource grouping versus execution: what is shared and what is private](#/comp4736-p4/classical-thread-model).
per process items|shared items: Items "shared by all threads in a process": Address space, Global variables, Open files, Child processes, Pending alarms, Signals and signal handlers, Accounting information. See [Resource grouping versus execution: what is shared and what is private](#/comp4736-p4/classical-thread-model).
per thread items|private items: Items "private to each thread": Program counter, Registers, Stack, State. See [Resource grouping versus execution: what is shared and what is private](#/comp4736-p4/classical-thread-model).
thread's stack: "Each thread has its own stack". See [Resource grouping versus execution: what is shared and what is private](#/comp4736-p4/classical-thread-model).
thread states: "running, blocked, ready, or terminated"; transitions "are the same as those between process states". See [Resource grouping versus execution: what is shared and what is private](#/comp4736-p4/classical-thread-model).
running (thread): "currently has the CPU and is active". See [Resource grouping versus execution: what is shared and what is private](#/comp4736-p4/classical-thread-model).
blocked (thread): "waiting for some event to unblock it", e.g. a system call to read from the keyboard blocks "until input is typed". See [Resource grouping versus execution: what is shared and what is private](#/comp4736-p4/classical-thread-model).
ready (thread): "scheduled to run and will as soon as its turn comes up". See [Resource grouping versus execution: what is shared and what is private](#/comp4736-p4/classical-thread-model).
terminated (thread): Listed as a thread state, not described. See [Resource grouping versus execution: what is shared and what is private](#/comp4736-p4/classical-thread-model).
multithreading: "the situation of allowing multiple threads in the same process"; "the CPU switches rapidly back and forth among the threads, providing the illusion that the threads are running in parallel, albeit on a slower CPU than the real one". See [Resource grouping versus execution: what is shared and what is private](#/comp4736-p4/classical-thread-model).
Pthreads|POSIX threads: "The threads package"; "Supported by most UNIX systems"; "Defines over 60 function calls". See [The Pthreads calls and the two-thread demo](#/comp4736-p4/pthreads).
pthread_create|Pthread_create: "Create a new thread". See [The Pthreads calls and the two-thread demo](#/comp4736-p4/pthreads).
pthread_exit|Pthread_exit: "Terminate the calling thread". See [The Pthreads calls and the two-thread demo](#/comp4736-p4/pthreads).
pthread_join|Pthread_join: "Wait for a specific thread to exit". See [The Pthreads calls and the two-thread demo](#/comp4736-p4/pthreads).
pthread_yield|Pthread_yield: "Release the CPU to let another thread run". See [The Pthreads calls and the two-thread demo](#/comp4736-p4/pthreads).
pthread_attr_init|Pthread_attr_init: "Create and initialize a thread's attribute structure". See [The Pthreads calls and the two-thread demo](#/comp4736-p4/pthreads).
pthread_attr_destroy|Pthread_attr_destro: "Remove a thread's attribute structure". See [The Pthreads calls and the two-thread demo](#/comp4736-p4/pthreads).
gettid|thread ID|TID: "gettid - get thread identification"; "returns the caller's thread ID (TID). In a single-threaded process, the thread ID is equal to the process ID … In a multithreaded process, all threads have the same PID, but each one has a unique TID". See [The Pthreads calls and the two-thread demo](#/comp4736-p4/pthreads).
user-level threads|implementing threads: "The threads package is put entirely in user space. The kernel knows nothing about them"; can be implemented on an OS "that does not support threads"; "threads are implemented by a library". See [Threads in user space, threads in the kernel](#/comp4736-p4/user-vs-kernel-threads).
run-time system: "a collection of procedures that manage threads e.g. pthread_create, pthread_exit, pthread_join, and pthread_yield"; manages the thread table. See [Threads in user space, threads in the kernel](#/comp4736-p4/user-vs-kernel-threads).
thread table: With user-space threads, each process's "own private thread table to keep track of the threads in that process", analogous to the kernel's process table but tracking "only … the per-thread properties, such as each thread's program counter, stack pointer, registers, state"; with kernel threads, "The kernel has a thread table that keeps track of all the threads in the system". See [Threads in user space, threads in the kernel](#/comp4736-p4/user-vs-kernel-threads).
process table: The kernel's table of processes; with kernel threads "The kernel also maintains the traditional process table to keep track of processes". See [Threads in user space, threads in the kernel](#/comp4736-p4/user-vs-kernel-threads).
user-level thread advantages: "No trap is needed, no context switch is needed, the memory cache need not be flushed … This makes thread scheduling very fast"; each process can have "its own customized scheduling algorithm"; "They also scale better". See [Threads in user space, threads in the kernel](#/comp4736-p4/user-vs-kernel-threads).
blocking system call problem: In user-level packages, letting a thread make a blocking call (e.g. read the keyboard before any keys are hit) "is unacceptable, since this will stop all the threads". See [Threads in user space, threads in the kernel](#/comp4736-p4/user-vs-kernel-threads).
no clock interrupts (user-level problem): A running user-level thread keeps the CPU "unless the first thread voluntarily gives up the CPU"; "Within a single process, there are no clock interrupts", so round-robin is impossible. See [Threads in user space, threads in the kernel](#/comp4736-p4/user-vs-kernel-threads).
kernel-level threads|implementing thread: "No run-time system is needed"; "No thread table in each process"; the kernel's thread table tracks all threads; when a thread blocks the kernel can run another thread of the same process or of a different process. See [Threads in user space, threads in the kernel](#/comp4736-p4/user-vs-kernel-threads).
kernel thread advantages and disadvantag: "do not require any new, nonblocking system calls"; on a page fault the kernel can run another runnable thread of the process; "main disadvantage is that the cost of a system call is substantial". See [Threads in user space, threads in the kernel](#/comp4736-p4/user-vs-kernel-threads).
user-level vs kernel-level thread: User-level are "faster to create and manage", implemented "by a thread library at the user level", "generic and can run on any operating system", and "Multi-threaded applications cannot take advantage of multiprocessing"; kernel-level are "slower to create and manage", the "Operating system supports creation of Kernel threads", "specific to the operating system", and "Kernel routines themselves can be multithreaded". See [Threads in user space, threads in the kernel](#/comp4736-p4/user-vs-kernel-threads).
hybrid implementation: "use kernel-level threads and then multiplex user-level threads onto some or all of them"; "the programmer can determine how many kernel threads to use and how many user-level threads to multiplex on each one"; "the ultimate in flexibility"; "the kernel is aware of only the kernel-level threads and schedules those". See [Hybrid implementations: many-to-one, one-to-one, many-to-many](#/comp4736-p4/hybrid-models).
multiplexing user-level threads onto ker: "each kernel-level thread has some set of user-level threads that take turns using it". See [Hybrid implementations: many-to-one, one-to-one, many-to-many](#/comp4736-p4/hybrid-models).
many-to-one|many to one relationship: "many user threads to one kernel thread"; "All user threads within a process share the same kernel thread"; "Managed by the user-level thread library, and the kernel remains unaware of individual user threads"; easy creation but "a lack of true concurrency". See [Hybrid implementations: many-to-one, one-to-one, many-to-many](#/comp4736-p4/hybrid-models).
one-to-one|one to one relationship: "one user thread to one kernel thread"; "Each user thread has a dedicated kernel thread for execution"; "Provides true concurrency"; creating many kernel threads "can introduce overhead". See [Hybrid implementations: many-to-one, one-to-one, many-to-many](#/comp4736-p4/hybrid-models).
many-to-many|many to many relationship: "many user-level threads to many kernel-level threads"; "Multiple user threads are mapped onto an equal or smaller number of kernel threads"; "a balance between concurrency and thread creation overhead"; library and kernel "work together". See [Hybrid implementations: many-to-one, one-to-one, many-to-many](#/comp4736-p4/hybrid-models).
platform thread: Java thread "managed by the operating system"; has "its own stack, program counter, and registers"; "resource-intensive" to create and manage; "heavyweight"; one platform thread per OS kernel thread in the diagram. See [Java platform threads three ways, and virtual threads](#/comp4736-p4/java-threads).
extending the Thread class: Java Method 1, `class MyThread extends Thread` overriding `run()`, started with `start()`. See [Java platform threads three ways, and virtual threads](#/comp4736-p4/java-threads).
implementing the Runnable interface: Java Method 2, `class MyRunnable implements Runnable`, passed to `new Thread(new MyRunnable())`. See [Java platform threads three ways, and virtual threads](#/comp4736-p4/java-threads).
lambda expression thread: Java Method 3, `Runnable r = () -> { … };` passed to `new Thread(r, "T1")`. See [Java platform threads three ways, and virtual threads](#/comp4736-p4/java-threads).
virtual thread: "lightweight, user-space threads that are managed by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) itself, rather than relying on native operating system threads"; "much more memory-efficient"; suited to "high concurrency requirements"; still "require proper synchronization"; created with `Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(r1)`, `isVirtual()` returns true. See [Java platform threads three ways, and virtual threads](#/comp4736-p4/java-threads).
Project Loom: Virtual threads are "also known as "Project Loom" virtual threads", "a new concurrency mechanism introduced as an experimental feature in more recent versions of Java". See [Java platform threads three ways, and virtual threads](#/comp4736-p4/java-threads).
pop-up thread: "The arrival of a message causes the system to create a new thread to handle the message"; latency between arrival and processing "can be made very short"; "since they are brand new, they do not have any history—registers, stack, whatever—that must be restored", so it can be created quickly. See [Pop-up threads](#/comp4736-p4/pop-up-threads).
